title: A Grandpa's Second Chance: Why a Supreme Court Ruling Could Send Him Back to Prison
summary: Anthony Bailey is 61 years old. He drives a city bus in Indianapolis, goes to family barbecues, and plays card games with his grandkids. But two years ago, he was in a federal prison, where he'd been for 27 years. A judge let him out early through a program called compassionate release, which is for prisoners who are very sick, very old, or have other extraordinary reasons to go home. Bailey got a second chance—and he's made the most of it. 'I'm a productive citizen, I work hard,' he says. But now, the Supreme Court has said that program can't be used just because a sentence is really, really long. Bailey was given a huge sentence back in 1997 for a bank robbery and carjackings where no one was physically hurt. He says he totally regrets what he did. Prosecutors now want to send him back to prison, where he could stay until 2050—when he'd be nearly 86. His lawyer says that's ridiculous because he's not dangerous. Congress made punishments less harsh for similar crimes, but that change doesn't help people already in prison. Bailey is hoping and praying he gets to keep his life.
why_it_matters: This case shows how rules about punishment can change and affect people's lives, reminding us that laws aren't always fair and can impact families like Bailey's grandkids.

background_read: The Supreme Court is the highest court in the United States and makes final decisions about what the law means.
Compassionate release was created to reduce crowding in prisons and show mercy to elderly or very sick prisoners.
Long prison sentences for crimes that didn't hurt anyone physically have been debated for many years.
Article_Structure: WHO: Anthony Bailey, a 61-year-old bus driver and former federal prisoner.
WHAT: He was released early under compassionate release but could be sent back to prison because of a new Supreme Court decision.
WHERE: Bailey lives in Indianapolis; he was imprisoned in a federal prison.
WHY: The Supreme Court said compassionate release can't be granted just because a sentence is very long, and prosecutors argue Bailey's long sentence should be fully served.

perspectives.description: They say he is no longer dangerous, works hard as a bus driver, and has built a good life. They believe sending him back to prison is cruel and pointless.

perspectives.perspective: Prosecutors and some crime victims' advocates
perspectives.description: They argue Bailey committed serious crimes and should serve the full sentence the judge gave him, because that's what the law said was fair at the time.
They point out that Congress changed the law for future cases but didn't make it apply to people already in prison, leaving prisoners like Bailey stuck in a gap between old and new rules.
